# Impact of Graphene Oxide Arrangement on the Mechanical and Viscoelastic Properties of Polymer Nanocomposites

**Authors:** Yitong Chen; Zhangke Yang; Linjiale Dai; Zhaoxu Meng

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Mechanical Engineering, Clemson University, Clemson, SC, 29631, USA

## Abstract

Graphene oxide (GO) is a promising reinforcing nanofiller for polymer nanocomposites due to its exceptional strength and strong adhesion to polymers. Despite extensive research, the effects of GO sheet arrangement and oxidation profiles on the mechanical and viscoelastic properties of these nanocomposites remain underexplored, and the underlying deformation mechanisms have not been explicitly unveiled. In this study, we employ coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations to investigate how distinct GO arrangements (separated vs. stacked sheets), varying interfacial interactions, and a range of oxidation profiles impact the mechanical and viscoelastic properties of GO-polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) nanocomposites. Our findings reveal that GO sheet arrangement plays a crucial role in determining the mechanical properties of nanocomposites, with separated GO sheets typically resulting in higher elastic and shear moduli due to increased interfacial area and stronger nanoconfinement effects. Additionally, stronger interfacial interactions enhance these moduli, with oxidation degree playing a complex role by simultaneously weakening GO’s intrinsic stiffness. Under shear deformation, stacked GO cases exhibit inter-sheet sliding, driven by weaker GO inter-sheet interactions and stronger GO-PMMA adhesion. The inter-sheet sliding enhances the loss modulus and loss tangent of the GO-PMMA nanocomposites, with the sliding magnitude directly correlating with the dynamic moduli. Our results indicate that polymers reinforced with stacked GO sheets can achieve superior damping capability through the activation of GO inter-sheet sliding. This makes them particularly suitable for applications requiring enhanced energy dissipation. This study highlights the pivotal role of GO arrangement in shaping the mechanical and viscoelastic behavior of polymer nanocomposites, providing valuable insights for tailored nanocomposite design.

## Introduction

Natural materials possess unique hierarchical microstructures that significantly enhance their mechanical properties, providing unparalleled insights for designing new materials [1-8]. For example, the beta-sheet nanocrystal reinforcement in spider and silkworm silk granted them high stiffness, strength and toughness [9, 10]. The periodic Bouligand structure and porous nanoparticles with interpenetrating biopolymers found in the dactyl club of mantis shrimp contribute to exceptional impact resistance [2, 3, 11]. The hierarchical structure integrating collagen fibrils and hydroxyapatite platelets enables bone to achieve the optimal balance of strength, toughness, and flexibility [12, 13]. Similarly, nacre, commonly referred to as the mother-of-pearl, demonstrates a remarkable amalgamation of strength and toughness [14, 15]. This is mainly attributed to its distinct nanolayered structure, which comprises ~95 vol% hard aragonite platelets that are closely stacked and staggered between adjacent layers and embedded within the ~5 vol% soft biopolymer matrix [15, 16].

A key principle derived from natural materials is the effective integration of nanoscale soft and hard phases, which helps overcome the traditional tradeoff between strength and toughness commonly found in conventional engineering materials. By drawing inspiration from natural materials and understanding the effective methods of integrating nanotechnological-enabled building blocks, we can transform the development of high-performance nanocomposite materials for applications in lightweight body armor [17, 18], vehicle [19], and spacecraft [20]. In fact, numerous experimental studies have been conducted to fabricate nanocomposites using advanced building blocks by adopting bioinspired structures. Particularly, graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice with hybridized s p 2 C-C bonding, is the strongest material identified to date ( E ∼ 1 TPa and strength ~ 130 GPa) [21]. It has proven to be an outstanding ‘hard’ nanofiller for enhancing the mechanical properties of polymers. Numerous studies have reported that graphene can dramatically enhance stiffness and strength at very low loadings compared to other nanofillers [22-27]. However, many studies reported that the incorporation of graphene restricts the movement of polymer chains or leads to local stress concentrations, consequently resulting in reduced failure strain and toughness of nanocomposites [28-31].

Despite graphene’s excellent reinforcement capabilities, its potential in polymer nanocomposites is often limited due to weak adhesion with polymer matrices. Graphene oxide (GO), a chemically modified derivative of graphene, offers an effective alternative by providing better interfacial adhesion with polymers, which significantly enhances the stiffness and strength of polymer nanocomposites [32-36]. It consists of epoxide, hydroxyl, and carboxyl functional groups on the basal plane of the 2D sheet, which significantly enhance the adhesion between various polymers and GO. The increased layer spacing and, thus, lower inter-sheet interaction among GO sheets further enhance the dispersibility of GO in a broad spectrum of solvents [37]. Although several experimental studies have indicated that incorporating GO can reduce nanocomposite’s extensibility [28, 34, 38-40], a study by Xu and colleagues revealed that GO-polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) films with homogeneously dispersed and uniquely layered GO sheets demonstrated improvements in stiffness, strength, and ultimate strain compared to neat PVA. Similarly, Chathuranga et al. fabricated GO-poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) nanocomposites with a nacre-like “brick and mortar” microstructure, resulting in 55% stronger and 42% tougher than other conventional GO-PMMA nanocomposites [41]. These studies highlight the potential of tailored GO arrangements in influencing the mechanical properties of polymer nanocomposites. Regarding the impact of oxidation levels of GO sheets on the mechanical properties of nanocomposites, Aradhana et al. compared epoxy nanocomposite filled with GO and reduced graphene oxide (rGO) [42]. rGO, derived from chemically or thermally treated GO, has fewer functional groups compared to GO [25]. This reduction in functional groups causes rGO to have relatively weaker adhesion with polymer matrices compared to GO, leading to easier sliding at the interface of GO and epoxy. Their findings indicated that, with the same wt%, nanocomposites reinforced with GO outperformed those reinforced with rGO across all metrics, including Young’s modulus, tensile strength at break, shear modulus, and impact strength.

While experimental studies have yielded valuable insights into the mechanical properties of GO-polymer nanocomposites, the variability in experimental results suggests that the effects of GO’s arrangement and oxidation level on mechanical properties warrant further investigation, particularly at smaller spatiotemporal scales.

Conversely, computational modeling serves as a powerful tool for elucidating the fundamental deformation mechanisms and mechanical properties of various materials, beginning at the molecular level [2, 43-45]. This approach allows for detailed investigations into how structural characteristics and interfacial interactions influence the mechanical behaviors of graphene-based nanocomposites [46-51]. In a recent comprehensive review, Talapatra et al. have identified key factors influencing the mechanical properties of nanocomposites such as the size, shape, arrangement and dispersion of nanofillers, along with their weight percentage and functionalization [52]. Additionally, Skountzos et al. investigated the mechanical properties of graphene/GO-PMMA nanocomposite through all-atomistic (AA) molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. They found that the GO sheets can enhance Young’s modulus, bulk modulus, and shear modulus of PMMA more than pure graphene sheets do. Rahman and Haque employed AA MD simulations to study the effect of graphene concentrations and agglomeration on the mechanical properties of graphene-epoxy nanocomposites. Their results showed that the nanocomposites tend to have a higher Young’s modulus with dispersed graphene compared to agglomerated graphene systems [47]. Zhang et al. also employed AA MD simulations and found that the mechanical performance of GO/graphene-reinforced nanocomposites depends on the conformation and the content of the intercalated polymer molecules [48]. Furthermore, Shiu et al. found intercalated GO fakes lead to a higher local polymer density near the graphene interface compared to clustered graphene oxide flakes, which leads to higher Young’s modulus, increased glass transition temperature, and reduced coefficient of thermal expansion in GO/epoxy nanocomposites through AA MD simulations [51]. Although AA MD simulations provide high resolution at the molecular level and detailed insights into associated mechanisms, the spatiotemporal scale they can reach is highly constrained.

In contrast, coarse-grained (CG) MD simulations can provide insights into systems at larger spatiotemporal scales while preserving essential molecular characteristics [2, 45, 53-55]. For example, Singh et al. employed CG models of stacked graphene/polyethylene to study the effect of shear strain rate, finding that nanocomposites exhibit frequency-dependent viscoelastic behavior [50]. Our group has extensively employed CG MD simulations to investigate the mechanical properties of graphene/GO-reinforced polymer nanocomposites [1, 46, 50, 56, 57]. For instance, one of our recent studies showed that the wrinkles in graphene sheets can lead to tensile stiffness reduction but enhancement in the damping of graphene-PMMA nanocomposite [57]. Another study investigated interfacial mechanics and viscoelastic properties of patchy GO-polybutadiene nanocomposites, and the results showed that the heterogeneous patchy structures on GO sheets have a nontrivial effect on these properties [46]. Moreover, we have also studied the impact of varying interfacial interactions between graphene and polycarbonate and found that increasing interfacial interactions lead to a rise in both storage and loss moduli [58]. Despite prior studies on similar material systems, the effects of the arrangement of GO sheets (stacked vs. separated), as well as oxidation degree and type on the mechanical and viscoelastic properties of GO-based polymer nanocomposites have yet to be fully explored.

In this paper, we aim to address existing knowledge gaps by investigating the mechanical and viscoelastic properties of GO nanocomposites with explicit oxidation profiles and arrangement in GO. We also aim to unveil and quantify the underlying deformation mechanisms of such nanocomposites using CG-MD simulations. We begin by constructing GO-PMMA nanocomposite models with either stacked or separated arrangement of GO sheets featuring varying oxidation profiles. We then apply uniaxial tensile deformation, out-of-plane shear deformation, and small amplitude oscillatory shear (SAOS) deformations to comprehensively characterize the mechanical and viscoelastic properties of nanocomposites. Additionally, we examine how specific deformation mechanisms within the nanocomposites influence the observed changes in their mechanical and viscoelastic behavior.

## Materials and Methods

In this section, we first present the CG models for GO and PMMA and detail the derivation of their interfacial adhesion parameters. We then describe the nanocomposite system setup, including system dimensions, GO oxidation profiles, and GO sheet arrangement. Finally, we outline our simulation procedures and analytical methods employed to investigate the mechanical and viscoelastic properties of nanocomposites.

### CG models of GO and PMMA

The CG model of GO was developed by Meng et al.[59], building upon an earlier CG model of graphene[60]. The CG model of GO introduces new types of CG beads to represent hydroxyl oxidized and epoxide oxidized regions while maintaining the hexagonal lattice. The CG force field parameters were derived from density functional-based tight binding simulations on several benchmark cases. The CG model captures the unique influences of hydroxyl oxidation (AL, short for alcohol group) and epoxide-oxidation (EP) in the mechanical responses of the GO sheets, enabled by incorporating new types of bonded and non-bonded interactions. More details on the parameters of the force field for the CG model can be found in the original paper [59]. In our study, we model different oxidation profiles for GO sheets, considering four oxidation degrees for each oxidation type, ranging from 20% to 72% for AL and up to 80% for EP, consistent with our previous work [59]. To implement these oxidation profiles in the simulations, we used an in-house code to randomly assign the appropriate number of oxidized beads within each GO sheet, ensuring that the desired oxidation degree was accurately represented in the structure files.

The PMMA CG model was developed by Hsu et al. [61], which utilizes a two-bead per monomer mapping strategy, with each repeating monomer consisting of a methacrylate backbone bead and a side-group bead. This model incorporates both bonded potentials (including bonds, angles, and dihedrals) and non-bonded interactions, with parameters obtained via the inverse Boltzmann method. Further details can be found in the original paper [61]. PMMA was chosen as the matrix material for our study mainly due to its widespread use as the matrix material for nanocomposites [62-65] and its molecular feature that represents the fundamental characteristics of a broad category of polymer materials [61].

The 12 – 6 Lennard-Jones (LJ) nonbonded potential is used to define the interfacial interactions between GO beads and polymer beads: (1) E g p = 4 ε g p [ ( σ g p r ) 12 − ( σ g p r ) 6 ] .

We use the following strategy for selecting LJ potential parameters to capture different binding energies between three types of GO beads and polymer chains, accommodating a wide range of polymeric systems. The interaction strength between graphitic beads and polymer beads is varied with ε gp = 0.8 , 1.2, and 1.6 kcal/mol for weak, medium, and strong interaction cases, respectively, with σ g p set as a constant of 4.5 Å. This results in interfacial energy values of approximately 0.15, 0.2, and 0.26 J ∕ m 2 between pure graphene sheet and polymer matrix, aligning with the experimental results [66]. We note that we focus on adhesive interfaces in this study, in consistent with our previous modeling studies on graphene-based nanocomposites [46, 57]. Previous investigations further showed that the interfacial binding energy between GO and polymers is approximately 40%-50% greater than that between graphene and polymers [67]. Additionally, EP exhibits marginally higher interfacial binding energy with polymers compared to AL [68]. Therefore, we adjust ε gp between AL and polymer beads and between EP and polymer beads to be 1.4 and 1.6 times higher, respectively, to reflect the differences in interactions across all cases. We believe such a setting enables us to examine different overall interactions between GO and polymer matrices while also capturing the ranking of GO-polymer interactions based on oxidation types and degrees.

### Nanocomposite model setup

The nanocomposite models used in this study consist of two GO sheets embedded in a continuous polymer matrix, constituting a representative volume element in a typical GO-reinforced polymer nanocomposite. The density of PMMA used in this study is 1.18 g/cm2 with each chain comprising 100 monomers, the same as our previous work [57]. We consider two different arrangements of GO sheets: stacked and separated cases, as shown in Fig 1(a) and Fig 1(b). The separated GO arrangement used here corresponds to well-dispersed GO sheets, which is highly desirable for enhancing mechanical properties but can be difficult to achieve experimentally due to GO's inherent tendency to aggregate [69]. In contrast, stacked arrangements commonly result from GO aggregation, which becomes increasingly difficult to prevent at higher GO loadings [70].

The simulation box has periodic boundary conditions (PBCs) in all three directions. The dimensions of the box in the x, y, and z directions are approximately 26 nm, 5 nm, and 14 nm, respectively. The GO sheets have a finite length of 20 nm in the x-direction as they are shorter than the dimension of the box and an infinite length in the y-direction with the addition of periodic bonds and the use of PBCs. Our intention for having an infinite length along the y-direction is to eliminate size effects and approximate the behavior of very large GO sheets in that direction. This allows us to focus on the fundamental effects of GO arrangement and oxidation profiles while avoiding artificial size effects imposed by finite sheet dimensions in the y-direction. We assume each GO sheet to have an effective thickness of 0.75 nm, which is consistent with previous studies [59, 71]. Thus, the volume fraction of GO is estimated to be around 8%, similar to our previous study [57] and other experimental studies [33, 72].

### Simulation methods

All MD simulations in this study are carried out by Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator (LAMMPS) software (Jun23_2022 version) [73]. The trajectories are visualized through the Visual Molecular Dynamics software [74].

We first minimize the energy of the system using the conjugate gradient algorithm. Subsequently, we equilibrate the system through an isothermal-isobaric (NPT) ensemble for a total of 1.2 ns, with a constant pressure of 0 atm in all directions and a temperature profile mimicking the annealing process: the temperature is first maintained at 300 K for 0.2 ns, then increased to 600 K over 0.2 ns, held at 600 K for another 0.2 ns, before decreased to 300 K over 0.2 nanoseconds, and finally stabilized at 300 K for an additional 0.2 nanoseconds. After the equilibration procedure, non-equilibrium MD simulations are conducted to investigate the mechanical and viscoelastic properties of the nanocomposites. A triclinic (non-orthogonal) simulation box is used to apply strains in the xz-direction for shear deformation.

We first characterize Young’s modulus or elastic modulus of the nanocomposite depending on GO sheet oxidation profiles and arrangements. A uniaxial tensile deformation is exerted in the x-direction at a constant nominal strain rate of 5 × 108 s−1 up to a strain of 0.1. During the tensile deformation, the NPT ensemble is used to maintain the pressure at 0 atm in y and z directions and the temperature at 300K. Each nanocomposite model with a specific oxidation profile and arrangement undergoes 20 simulation runs with different initial conditions to account for statistical variances. Young’s modulus is calculated by linear fitting of the stress-strain curves from 0 to 0.01 strain. We report both the average values and standard deviations (error bar) of Young’s modulus results of different nanocomposites.

To quantitatively compare how GO sheets enhance the Young’s modulus of the nanocomposite while accounting for the differences in elastic modulus of GO sheets themselves, we also calculate the reinforcing efficiency parameter ( ξ ) parameter for each nanocomposite model according to the Halpin-Tsai equation [75]. ξ can be derived using the following equation: (2) ξ = E G O ( E ∗ − E m ) − V G O E ∗ ( E G O − E m ) E m [ ( E G O − E ∗ ) − V m ( E G O − E m ) ] , where E GO is the in-plane elastic modulus of GO sheets, E m is the elastic modulus of PMMA matrix, E ∗ is the measured elastic modulus of the nanocomposite, V GO is the volume ratio of GO sheets, and V m is the matrix volume ratio which equals to 1 − V GO . We note that the volume ratios remain constant across all nanocomposite models in this study, as they consist of the same numbers of polymer chains and GO sheets.

Next, out-of-plane shear deformation is applied to nanocomposites in the xz-direction at a constant strain rate of 5 × 10 8 s − 1 . The NPT ensemble is also applied during the shear test, with the temperature maintained at 300K. Similarly, we conduct 20 shear tests on each nanocomposite up to a 0.1 shear strain and calculate shear modulus by fitting the strain range from 0 to 0.01.

Last, we apply small amplitude oscillatory shear (SAOS) test in the out-of-plane xz-direction to investigate the viscoelastic behavior of nanocomposites [46]. The NVT/SLLOD ensemble is used during the SAOS test, while maintaining the temperature at 300K. This specific ensemble adjusts the bead positions and velocities to create a velocity profile that aligns with the change in box size and shape. In addition, we activate the “remap v” option to remap bead velocities as they cross periodic boundaries, ensuring they stay consistent with the velocity profile. We apply a sinusoidal strain which can be expressed as a function of time γ xz ( t ) = γ 0 sin ( ω t ) , where γ 0 is the shear strain amplitude and ω is the frequency. We select γ 0 to be 0.05 and ω to be 2 × 1010 Hz, in consensus with our previous studies [46, 57]. We acknowledge that the measured dynamic moduli can vary with frequency. Singh PP, et al. demonstrated that dynamic moduli of graphene-based nanocomposites exhibit a monatomic trend with increasing frequency in the range of 109 to 1011 Hz [50]. Our chosen frequency falls within this range and aligns with our previous studies on the viscoelastic properties of nanocomposites [46, 76], ensuring methodological consistency and comparability across investigations.

Due to the viscoelastic behavior of the nanocomposites, the resulting stress output is mathematically related to the shear strain as: (3) σ x z ( t ) = σ 0 sin ( ω t + δ ) ,

Each nanocomposite is tested 20 times with different initial states, and each test includes 15 cycles of oscillation. To account for potential stress instability, the initial 5 cycles of stress-strain data are discarded. To model the output stress from the subsequent 10 cycles, a nonlinear curve-fitting function in MATLAB is utilized to derive stress amplitude ( σ 0 ) and phase lag ( δ ). Consequently, storage modulus ( G ′ ), loss modulus ( G ″ ), and tangent loss ( tan ( δ ) ) can be calculated using the following equations: (4) G ′ = σ 0 γ 0 cos ( δ ) , (5) G ″ = σ 0 γ 0 sin ( δ ) , (6) and tan ( δ ) = G ″ G ′ .

## Results and Discussions

In this section, we systematically investigate the effects of GO sheet arrangement (separated vs. stacked) and oxidation profiles (type and degree) on the mechanical and viscoelastic properties of GO-PMMA nanocomposites. First, we evaluate the elastic modulus of nanocomposites under tensile deformation, highlighting the role of GO dispersion and interfacial interactions in enhancing stiffness. Next, we explore the shear response, where inter-sheet sliding in stacked GO configurations leads to unique deformation behaviors. We then examine the viscoelastic properties through SAOS simulations, revealing the impact of GO arrangement on dynamic moduli.

### Dependence of Young’s modulus on GO arrangement and oxidation profile.

In this section, we examine the effect of GO sheet oxidation profiles and arrangements on Young’s modulus of the nanocomposites. Representative stress-strain curves for each distinct configuration are presented in Fig. 2. We choose ε gp = 1.2 kcal ∕ mol to showcase here since it is the median of all ε gp values employed in this study. However, we confirm that the curves for other ε gp values exhibit similar behaviors. It is important to note that, across all ε gp values examined in this study, the sliding at the interface of polymer and GO is minimal during tensile deformation of the nanocomposites, indicating efficient interfacial stress transfer [77]. As a result, the mechanical properties of the nanocomposites are primarily governed by the intrinsic properties of the fillers and their nanoconfinement effect on the PMMA matrix.

The average Young’s modulus for each nanocomposite is depicted in Fig. 3, with error bars representing the standard deviation from 20 runs. The results are organized into four panels by unique oxidation type (AL vs. EP) and arrangement (Stacked vs. Separated), with comparisons made across varying oxidation degrees. Additionally, average ξ values with error bars are plotted in purple, aligning with the right y-axis in Fig. 3. To calculate ξ using Eq. 2, we directly use the values for E m and E G O from the original works [59, 61]. Specifically, the E m is 3.3 GPa, and the E GO values for AL GO and EP GO range from 423 to 297 GPa and 409 to 237 GPa, respectively. We note that Young’s moduli of the GO sheets in this study might slightly differ from the original values due to minor differences in the oxidation distribution and size of the GO sheets. Nevertheless, we ensure that the functional groups are randomly distributed, adhering to the same approach in the previous work [46], and previous studies have shown that the oxidation degree is the primary factor in affecting GO’s in-plane mechanical properties [78, 79].

When comparing Fig. 3(a)(b) with (c)(d), nanocomposites with separated GO sheets exhibit higher Young’s moduli across all oxidation profiles and ε gp values than their stacked counterparts. This is primarily due to the greater interfacial area available between GO sheets and polymer in separated configurations. In contrast, in stacked cases, the contact area is relatively smaller since one side of the GO sheet is mostly in contact with its adjacent GO sheet. In general, a larger interfacial area enhances the nanoconfinement effect on the polymer, thereby increasing the Young’s modulus of the nanocomposite [10, 80-82]. Additionally, for the same oxidation degree and arrangement of GO, Young’s modulus of nanocomposite increases with ε gp . This is consistent with previous studies indicating that stronger interfacial interactions between nanofillers and polymer leads to enhanced nanoconfinement effects and, thus, higher moduli of nanocomposites [83, 84]. Similar trends are also observed for the dependence of ξ on the arrangement of GO sheets and ε gp , indicating the ξ factor is directly related to the nanoconfinement effect.

In comparison to GO arrangements and ε gp , oxidation degree has a subtler yet more nuanced impact on Young’s modulus of the nanocomposites. Specifically, for AL GO, there is a slight increase in Young’s modulus observed for stacked GO and separated GO with higher ε gp , though this trend is not clear for separated GO with lower ε gp values, as shown in Fig.3(a)(c). Conversely, the average Young’s moduli of EP GO nanocomposites exhibit a slight downward trend with increasing oxidation degrees, as illustrated in Fig.3(b)(d). This decrease in modulus for EP GO, despite stronger interfacial interactions from increased oxidation, is due to the significant drop in the intrinsic elastic modulus of GO, which overwhelms the benefits of enhanced nanoconfinement. Specifically, E GO of EP GO shows a faster decay as the oxidation degree increases compared to AL, as captured in the CG model of GO [59]. In general, increasing the nanoconfinement effect and decreasing E G O has a competing effect on the overall Young’s modulus of the nanocomposite. This observation aligns with the findings presented by Jie et al. to a certain extent, wherein they reported a decrease in Young’s modulus of GO/epoxy nanocomposites as the oxidation level of GO rises [85].

We then compare ξ values for varying oxidation degrees, serving as quantitative indicators of reinforcing efficiency while discounting the influence of the elastic modulus of the fillers [75]. Interestingly, ξ values generally increase with oxidation degree, supporting the enhanced nanoconfinement effect of GO sheets with increasing functional group coverages on polymer matrix [86, 87]. We note that the increasing trend of ξ with oxidation degree is more pronounced for separated GO cases compared to stacked cases, highlighting the crucial role of interface area (or dispersion quality of nanofillers) for achieving effective reinforcement. Additionally, in separated cases, ξ shows a more marked increase with ε gp = 1.6 kcal/mol compared to lower ε gp values, indicating the beneficial impact of stronger interfacial interactions on reinforcing efficiency.

### Dependence of shear responses on GO arrangement and oxidation profile.

In this section, we explore the effect of the GO oxidation profile and arrangement on the out-of-plane shear response of the GO nanocomposites. Representative shear stress-strain curves for different nanocomposites with ε gp = 1.2 kcal/mol are shown in Fig. 4. Notably, there are large stress drops uniquely present in stacked cases during shear deformation. To make sure the shear modulus calculation is not affected by the noticeable stress drops, we use a relatively small strain range (<0.01) for the calculations.

Upon examining the simulation trajectories, we observe sliding events between GO sheets in stacked arrangement. In our previous study, we noted a similar behavior occurring in the bilayer graphene-PMMA nanocomposite with graphene possessing a wrinkled arrangement during shear deformation [57]. A similar large stress drop also occurred during out-of-plane shear deformation due to lower shear resistance induced by the wrinkled arrangement. Herein, we further observe that sliding between GO sheets can be easily activated due to the larger inter-sheet spacing and decreased inter-sheet shear resistance. We conclude that the large stress drops in Fig. 4. for the stacked arrangement GO nanocomposites are directly associated with this GO sliding event, attributing to the weak adhesion between the GO sheets.

Next, we compare the shear modulus of nanocomposites. As shown in Fig. 5, the separated GO nanocomposites possess a higher shear modulus than their stacked counterparts. This difference is primarily due to the greater interfacial area with polymer chains in separated GO sheets, enhancing the nanoconfinement effect. Additionally, stacked GO sheets exhibit internal instability, which could diminish their reinforcement effect on the shear modulus [88, 89]. While the intrinsic mechanical properties of nanofillers influence the shear response, it is the nanoconfinement effect that plays a more significant role. Additionally, we also observed a slight increase in the average shear modulus of the nanocomposites as ε gp and oxidation level increase, attributing to the enhanced nanoconfinement of the polymer. Aradhana et al. observed a similar trend in their GO-PVA nanocomposites, where thermally-reduced GO-PVA nanocomposites exhibited a lower shear modulus compared to those reinforced with highly oxidized GO [42]. We note that the observed difference is not pronounced due to data variability, but we expect the difference to become more apparent with larger GO sizes [85].

### Viscoelastic properties of nanocomposites depending on GO arrangement and oxidation profile.

In this section, we investigate the viscoelastic behavior of nanocomposites using SAOS at a frequency of 2 × 1010 Hz, following methodologies from our previous studies [46, 57]. Fig. 6(a) depicts the sinusoidal oscillatory shear process, and Fig. 6(b) shows typical stress and strain data over 2 periods of oscillation. There is a phase lag ( δ ) between the crests of the stress curve and the strain curve. δ indicates the viscous behavior of the nanocomposite system. Dynamic moduli ( G ′ , G ″ , and tan ( δ ) ) can be derived from σ 0 using Eq. 3-6 in Section 2.3. While G ′ assesses the elastic response of a material under deformation, G ″ represents the viscous portion of the response and tan ( δ ) provides a measure of damping in the material. A higher tan ( δ ) value indicates a higher damping capability of the material, which is more favorable for applications requiring a higher level of energy dissipation [90, 91].

We show the dynamic moduli of nanocomposites with separated GO sheets in Fig. 7. We observe slight enhancement of both G ′ and G ″ values with increasing ε g p , while tan ( δ ) remains consistent, indicating no significant change in the damping capability of the nanocomposite with increasing interfacial interactions between GO and polymer chains. Similar trends in viscoelastic behaviors of GO-PVA nanocomposites are also observed in the experimental work by Aradhana et al. [42]. The dynamic moduli are very similar for both AL and EP nanocomposites under the same ε gp and oxidation degree. Additionally, dynamic moduli show negligible changes with varying oxidation degrees, suggesting minimal impact from oxidation type and degree on the viscoelastic properties of nanocomposites with separated GO sheets. Since we observe minimal sliding at the interface of GO and PMMA, thus, energy is primarily dissipated through the sliding among polymer chains. The relatively small values of tan ( δ ) corroborate the glassy behavior of the polymer matrix. Furthermore, we note that the observed minor difference might be attributed to the small size of the model system. We anticipate the difference potentially becoming more pronounced with larger GO sizes.

Next, we investigate the viscoelastic behaviors of nanocomposites with stacked GO sheets. Dynamic moduli result of stacked arrangement nanocomposites are shown in Fig. 8. G ′ increases with increased oxidation degree and ε gp values, especially from 0.8 to 1.2 kcal/mol. The increase in G ′ is attributed to the overall enhanced nanoconfinement effect from stronger interfacial interactions. EP GO nanocomposites display higher G ′ compared to AL GO nanocomposites due to greater interfacial binding strength. Conversely, G ″ does not show strong dependency on ε g p and oxidation degree by considering the data variability, except that there is a minor decreasing trend in G ″ with oxidation degree at higher ε gp values, which can be similarly explained by the reasons for the separated cases.

Generally, tan ( δ ) decreases with an increase in ε gp and oxidation degree at higher ε gp values (i.e., ε gp = 1.2 or 1.6 kcal/mol), reflecting increased elastic behavior at the cost of less prominent viscous behavior due to stronger nanoconfinement. Nevertheless, G ″ and tan ( δ ) in stacked cases also show unusual patterns that are not solely explained by nanoconfinement at polymer-GO interfaces. Notably, tan ( δ ) values in stacked cases are significantly higher than those in separated cases presented in Fig. 7(e) and (f), with some configurations exceeding the value of 1, indicating the presence of additional dissipation mechanisms in the stacked cases. Additionally, an odd pattern emerges at ε gp = 0.8 , where tan ( δ ) increases as the oxidation degree goes from 20% to 40%, particularly for the AL case, before a subsequent decrease in tan ( δ ) with further oxidation. These unusual patterns prompt a detailed investigation into the deformation mechanisms under SAOS.

### Critical role of GO inter-sheet sliding.

Upon analyzing the simulation trajectories, it is observed that stacked GO sheets slide continuously in nanocomposites during SAOS deformation. This is reasonable as the strain amplitude during SAOS typically exceeds the strain thresholds where sliding occurs, as depicted in Fig. 4. Interestingly, the sliding distance mirrors the sinusoidal nature of the applied oscillatory strain, confirming continuous sliding. Fig. 9(c) and Fig. 9(d) illustrate sliding distance vs. shear strain for more viscous and more elastic nanocomposites, respectively, corresponding to the stress and shear strain relationships shown in Fig. 9(a) and Fig. 9(b). A shorter sliding distance in Fig. 9(c) correlates with a lower tangent loss and more elastic behavior in Fig. 9(a), whereas a more significant sliding distance in Fig. 9(d) leads to increased viscous behavior in Fig. 9(b). This sliding mechanism is identified as a primary contributor to the higher tan ( δ ) values and enhanced energy dissipation in nanocomposites with a stacked GO arrangement [92].

We further evaluate the oscillatory sliding distance ( Δ ) during SAOS by measuring the amplitude of a fitted sinusoidal curve, similar to the treatment of the stress data, as demonstrated in Fig. 10(a). The comparisons of Δ across different nanocomposite configurations are shown in Fig. 10(b). Remarkably, the pattern of Δ among different configurations is consistent with that of tan ( δ ) . For example, at ε g p = 0.8 kcal/mol, Δ and tan ( δ ) both peak at an oxidation degree of 40% for both AL and EP. The peak of Δ at moderate oxidation degree can be attributed to the balance between the interfacial shear strength at the polymer/GO interface and the inter-sheet shear strength within stacked GO sheets. For a relatively weak interface by using ε g p = 0.8 k c a l ∕ m o l , an initial increase of oxidation degree enhances the shear stress transfer at the polymer/GO interface, thus increasing the magnitude of Δ As oxidation degree further rises, the increasing of the inter-sheet strength becomes more dominant, which has a negative impact on the magnitude of Δ . Notably, the nanocomposite with 80% EP at ε gp = 1.6 kcal/mol has the smallest Δ , and this case also exhibits the lowest tan ( δ ) .

The strong correlation between Δ and damping capability ( tan ( δ ) ) suggests that GO inter-sheet sliding is a key energy dissipation mechanism uniquely present in nanocomposites with stacked GO sheets. Despite generally lower elastic and shear moduli in these composites due to reduced exposure of GO basal planes, our results show that such arrangement can significantly enhance the damping capability of GO-PMMA nanocomposites through the activation of GO inter-sheet sliding, making them highly suitable for specific applications that require improved damping or energy dissipation [90, 91].

### Discussions on insights, limitations, and future work

The findings from our study provide direct guidance on how GO sheet arrangement and oxidation profiles influence the bulk properties of GO-polymer nanocomposites. Specifically, our results demonstrate that a uniform dispersion of GO monolayer sheets (Separated arrangement) enhances the elastic modulus, supporting the common experimental goal of achieving well-dispersed GO sheets in the polymer matrix for improved stiffness. Conversely, our findings reveal that stacked GO sheets significantly enhance damping capacity, albeit at the expense of reduced elastic modulus enhancement. This suggests that incorporating bilayer or multilayer GO sheets in polymer nanocomposites can be advantageous for applications where damping performance is a priority. We also note that fine-tuning GO’s oxidation profile while maintaining a desired structural arrangement presents significant challenges. Nevertheless, advancements in processing techniques, such as surface functionalization of GO, controlled solvent evaporation, and external shear-assisted methods [93-97], have shown promise in mitigating aggregation and improving dispersion in a more controllable manner. Continued development in these areas will be essential for optimizing the fabrication and properties of GO-based polymer nanocomposites.

Despite the valuable insights gained from this study, we acknowledge certain limitations in our current modeling approach. Our investigation focuses on a small representative volume element, while system complexity increases at larger scales due to local heterogeneities in GO arrangement, oxidation levels, and polymer interactions. The present work serves as a foundation for bridging to larger-scale investigations, which we plan to pursue in future studies. Additionally, we observe minimal sliding at the interface between GO and PMMA with a minimum ε g p = 0.8 kcal/mol, corresponding to an effective interfacial energy of around 0.15 J ∕ m 2 . However, weaker interfacial adhesion might exist between GO and other polymer types, potentially leading to more pronounced energy dissipation through GO-polymer interfacial sliding. Moreover, while our CG model employs the LJ potential to approximate interfacial interactions, real GO-polymer interactions can be more complex, involving specific chemical bonding, entanglements, and localized defects, which are not fully captured in this approach.

Furthermore, GO inter-sheet sliding is expected to be size-dependent, and based on the shear lag model [5, 98, 99], the energy barrier for activation may plateau at a critical sheet size. Other factors, such as temperature, shear frequency, loading conditions, system size, and the number of GO layers, could further influence the extent of inter-sheet sliding and the overall energy dissipation mechanisms. These aspects are critical considerations for optimizing the damping performance of GO-based nanocomposites.

To address these issues, our future work plans to vary the size of GO sheets, including the number of layers to assess the size dependence of inter-sheet sliding and explore its impact on the overall mechanical and viscoelastic properties of nanocomposites. We also plan to investigate a broader range of GO/polymer interfaces, incorporating defects, functional group variability, and a spectrum of interfacial strengths, including very weak and very strong interfaces, potentially with crosslinking bonds between GO sheets and polymer chains. Additionally, we will examine the effects of temperature, shear frequency, and number of GO layers in the stacked arrangement to further understand their impact on the mechanical and viscoelastic properties of nanocomposites [50]. Furthermore, our future work will apply combined tensile and shear deformations along with other complex loading conditions to thoroughly investigate nanocomposites’ mechanical and viscoelastic behaviors [50, 100]. Lastly, with the allowance of computational resources, we also plan to assess additional mechanical properties such as failure strength, toughness, and extensibility by applying greater strain values and look into the deformation mechanisms associated with the changes in these mechanical properties.

## Conclusions

In this study, we utilized CG MD to investigate the effect of GO arrangement and oxidation on mechanical and viscoelastic properties of polymer nanocomposites by using a representative model of GO-PMMA nanocomposite. This model allowed us to vary structural configurations and interfacial interactions between GO and polymer while capturing the impact of oxidation types and degrees on GO-polymer interactions. We particularly examined varying oxidation profiles of GO sheets and analyzed the distinct behaviors of stacked and separated GO arrangements that are commonly found in actual GO/polymer nanocomposites.

Our findings demonstrate that separated cases have higher Young’s modulus and shear modulus compared to stacked ones. In addition, a higher ε g p consistently enhances these properties. However, an increase in oxidation degree for the EP GO tends to decrease Young’s modulus due to the rapid deterioration of EP GO’s modulus. Nevertheless, the reinforcing efficiency ξ calculated from the Halpin-Tsai equation, generally increases with both ε gp and oxidation degree. Such findings highlight the role of nanoconfinement in strengthening nanocomposites. During out-of-plane shear deformation, large stress drops were observed for most of the nanocomposites with a stacked GO arrangement, which are correlated with GO inter-sheet sliding events. Such internal instability of the stacked GO sheets could diminish the reinforcement effect on the shear modulus. Subsequently, we carried out SAOS tests to examine the effect of GO arrangement and oxidation on the viscoelastic properties of nanocomposites. SAOS tests revealed that separated cases showed increased G ′ and G ″ with rising ε gp , while tan ( δ ) remains stable. Interestingly, stacked configurations exhibited significantly higher tan ( δ ) due to the activation of interlayer sliding of GO sheets, suggesting superior damping capabilities. tan ( δ ) peaks at moderate oxidation degree for the lowest ε gp cases. Higher ε gp typically leads to an increased G ′ , accompanied by reductions in both G ″ and tan ( δ ) . We discover a strong correlation between nanocomposites’ tan ( δ ) and Δ , indicating GO inter-sheet sliding is the predominant energy dissipation mechanism during SAOS. A possible reason for the peak of Δ and tan ( δ ) at moderate oxidation degree is the balance between the interfacial shear strength at the polymer/GO interface and the inter-sheet shear strength within stacked GO sheets.

In summary, our study shows that oxidation and arrangement of GO sheets significantly affect the mechanical and viscoelastic properties of nanocomposites. We also unravel underlying deformation mechanisms that explain these nuanced influences. These fundamental insights can guide the interpretation of experimental results and inform the design and fabrication of GO-polymer nanocomposites with desired properties.
